newsitem.title: PORTUGAL: SOCCER-UEFA AND CAF SIGN HISTORIC FRIENDSHIP ACCORD.
newsitem.headline: SOCCER-UEFA AND CAF SIGN HISTORIC FRIENDSHIP ACCORD.

text.p: UEFA and CAF, the bodies which control soccer in Europe and Africa respectively, formally ended years of barely concealed hostility towards one another when they signed an historic friendship agreement on Thursday.

The Convention, as it has been termed, was signed by Lennart Johansson, the Swedish president of the European football assocation, and Issa Hayatou of Cameroon, his counterpart in the Confederation of African Football.
"It is a neccesity for us to co-operate with each other in the future," Johansson said at the signing ceremony.

"Our two continents are close geographically, culturally and historically. As far as football is concerned we both have 50-odd members associations representing some 700 million people and football is the number one sport. Our ambition is to keep it like that in both of our continents."

Hayatou said: "I praise the spirit of co-operation with UEFA. Football is going to benefit, Africa is going to benefit and the many Africans playing the game and living in Europe are going to benefit."
The new convention ties the two confederations to "undertake extensive co-operation in all football-related matters as partners with equal rights.

"This co-operation shall be based on friendship and mutual respect and aims to promote the development of football on both continents. Furthermore, football throughout the world should benfit from this co-operation."

As a member of CAF's executive committee said on Wednesday, the day before the agreement was signed: "It is no secret that there have been times when Europe has acted against Africa's interests and the Africans have done the same to the Europeans. The time for that has past and we are now set on building bridges rather than creating more divisions between ourselves."
The first tangible impact of the new agreement will be felt immediatly in Namibia and Chad, two of the poorer African nations.
They have been selected as the first two countries to receive financial aid, equipment, transport and communication tools like faxes and computers as part of the new deal.
They will also receive special help with coaching and other technical assistance to help develop the game in their countries.

All of UEFA's aid will be given to CAF who will share it out accordingly. CAF will also receive the proceeds of Wednesday night's All Star Match in Lisbon in which Africa defeated Europe 2-1, and UEFA will meet all of CAF's costs for the fixture.

Though the crowd of 10,000 was hugely disappointing, heavy rain did not help. "But a good point was that the TV pictures went to more than 100 countries around the world and we shall not hesitate to stage a similiar match of that sort again," Johansson said.
The game will almost certainly become a two-yearly event with the next match staged in Africa in 1999.

As this week, it is likely to be staged in conjunction with the new Meridian Cup for national Under-17 teams which is being held in eight Portugese towns and cities over the next 10 days with a field comprising Ghana, Guinea, Ivory Coast and Nigeria from Africa and France, Greece, Portugal and Spain from Europe.

The two confederations will also try and work closely together over the issue of young African players moving to European clubs, which in some ways can financially benefit their families back home, but also creates social and sporting problems.
